images.caption: Peripheral smear in sickle cell disease. Deoxygenated HbS polymerises and bends red cells into rigid crescents that block small vessels and are cleared early by the spleen.
look_for: polychromatic (bluish) young red cells from marrow response
images.author: Ed Uthman from Houston, TX, USA
images.credit: Ed Uthman from Houston, TX, USA, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Severe iron deficiency: red cells are small and pale with a wide central halo because too little haemoglobin is made. Compare the cells with the lymphocyte nucleus, which is about the size of a normal red cell.
look_for: microcytic red cells smaller than a lymphocyte nucleus
hypochromia with central pallor over half the cell
images.author: Ed Uthman from Houston, TX, USA
images.credit: Ed Uthman from Houston, TX, USA, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Bone marrow packed with myeloblasts in acute myeloid leukaemia. Pink needle-like Auer rods in the blast cytoplasm are fused primary granules and point to a myeloid rather than lymphoid lineage.
look_for: sheets of large blasts with fine chromatin and nucleoli
thin pink Auer rods in the cytoplasm
images.author: Paulo Henrique Orlandi Mourao
images.credit: Paulo Henrique Orlandi Mourao, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Cross-section of a right coronary artery with a thick, eccentric atherosclerotic plaque that narrows the lumen. Plaques like this limit flow on exertion (stable angina) and can rupture to trigger thrombosis.
look_for: eccentric intimal thickening narrowing the lumen
intact media and adventitia outside the plaque
images.author: Nephron
images.credit: Nephron, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Thrombus from a fatal pulmonary embolism showing alternating pale bands of platelets and fibrin and darker bands of trapped red cells. These lines of Zahn show the clot formed in flowing blood before death, which separates it from a post-mortem clot.
images.author: Nephron
images.credit: Nephron, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: A healthy adult blood film: red cells of even size with a pale central third, two segmented neutrophils, a lymphocyte and scattered platelets. Use it as the baseline for judging size, colour and shape in every abnormal smear.
look_for: uniform round RBCs with central pallor about one third of the cell
small lymphocyte with a thin rim of cytoplasm
images.author: Keith Chambers
images.credit: Keith Chambers, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Thin blood film with Plasmodium falciparum ring forms inside red cells. Small delicate rings, sometimes two in one cell or sitting at the cell edge, with normal-sized host cells are typical of falciparum.
look_for: dot-like chromatin with a thin blue cytoplasmic ring
images.author: Dr Graham Beards
images.credit: Dr Graham Beards, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Whole lymph node from a colectomy specimen. The thin capsule, subcapsular sinus, outer cortex with follicles and the paler medulla are all visible, showing how lymph filters through the node.
look_for: fibrous capsule with subcapsular sinus beneath it
medullary cords and sinuses toward the hilum
images.author: Ed Uthman, MD
images.credit: Ed Uthman, MD, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: A reactive lymph node with an enlarged secondary follicle: a pale germinal centre ringed by a dark mantle zone of small B cells. Follicles that vary in size and keep a mantle and polarity favour a benign reaction over lymphoma.
look_for: pale germinal centre with mixed centroblasts and centrocytes
dark mantle zone cuffing the germinal centre
tingible-body macrophages in the germinal centre
images.author: Patho
images.credit: Patho, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: A Reed-Sternberg cell in classical Hodgkin lymphoma: a large cell with two mirror-image nuclei each holding a big eosinophilic nucleolus ('owl eyes'). The malignant cells are rare among a background of reactive lymphocytes and other inflammatory cells.
look_for: large binucleate cell with owl-eye nucleoli
images.author: Calicut Medical College
images.credit: Calicut Medical College, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Burkitt lymphoma: sheets of monotonous medium-sized B cells with scattered pale tingible-body macrophages, the classic 'starry sky'. The macrophages are clearing tumour cells that die at the high turnover driven by MYC translocation.
look_for: dense sheet of uniform medium-sized lymphoid cells (the 'sky')
images.author: Ed Uthman, MD
images.credit: Ed Uthman, MD, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Touch preparation of Burkitt lymphoma. The tumour cells have deep blue cytoplasm with many clear lipid vacuoles, a cytology clue that matches the starry-sky pattern seen in sections.
look_for: medium-sized cells with deeply basophilic cytoplasm
round nuclei with several small nucleoli
images.author: Ed Uthman, MD
images.credit: Ed Uthman, MD, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Tuberculous lymph node with caseous necrosis bordered by epithelioid macrophages and a Langhans giant cell. Caseation, the cheesy amorphous centre, is the hallmark of the cell-mediated response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
look_for: Langhans giant cell with horseshoe nuclei
images.author: Department of Pathology, Calicut Medical College
images.credit: Department of Pathology, Calicut Medical College, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Acid-fast bacilli of Mycobacterium tuberculosis stained red by Ziehl-Neelsen against a blue counterstain. The mycolic-acid-rich wall holds carbol fuchsin even after acid-alcohol decolourisation.
look_for: bacilli sometimes beaded or in small clumps
images.author: CDC/Dr. George P. Kubica
images.credit: CDC/Dr. George P. Kubica, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Gallyas silver stain of the hippocampus with black flame-shaped neurofibrillary tangles filling neuron cell bodies. Tangles are aggregates of hyperphosphorylated tau and their spread tracks cognitive decline.
look_for: black flame-shaped tangles in neuronal cytoplasm
tangles extending into the proximal dendrite
images.author: Patho
images.credit: Patho, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Tau immunostain in Alzheimer cortex. Brown tau fills neurons as tangles (arrow) and forms a cluster of dystrophic neurites around an amyloid plaque (arrowhead).
look_for: neuritic plaque ringed by tau-positive dystrophic neurites
images.author: Tulemo
images.credit: Tulemo, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: A pigmented substantia nigra neuron containing a Lewy body (arrowhead): a round eosinophilic inclusion with a pale halo. Lewy bodies are built from alpha-synuclein, and loss of these dopaminergic neurons causes the motor signs of Parkinson disease.
look_for: round pink cytoplasmic inclusion with a pale halo
images.author: Tulemo
images.credit: Tulemo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Alpha-synuclein immunostain marking a Lewy body as a dense brown ball inside a nigral neuron. The stain makes the inclusions easy to count and is how Lewy pathology is mapped through the brain.
images.author: Marvin 101
images.credit: Marvin 101, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Normal brain at the grey-white junction: neurons with triangular cell bodies and nucleoli sit in a pink fibrillary neuropil. Glial nuclei are small, round and dark, and the white matter beside it holds no neurons.
look_for: pyramidal neurons with visible nucleoli and Nissl substance
small dark oligodendrocyte and astrocyte nuclei
images.author: Nephron
images.credit: Nephron, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: A peripheral nerve fascicle cut across and stained with osmium, which blackens myelin lipid. Each dark ring is the myelin sheath around one axon; the fascicle is wrapped by perineurium.
look_for: black myelin rings around pale axons
images.author: Малишко Анастасія
images.credit: Малишко Анастасія, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Glioblastoma with serpiginous bands of necrosis lined by densely packed tumour nuclei (pseudopalisading). Tumour cells migrate away from hypoxic, thrombosed areas, and necrosis or microvascular proliferation marks a grade 4 astrocytic tumour.
look_for: crowded tumour nuclei lining the necrosis edge
hypercellular background of atypical glial cells
images.author: Jensflorian
images.credit: Jensflorian, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Multiple sclerosis lesion on a myelin stain: intact white matter is deep blue, and the sharply bordered plaque is pale because its myelin is lost. A lymphocytic cuff around a vein in the plaque shows the immune attack that drives demyelination.
look_for: sharp edge between blue myelinated and pale demyelinated white matter
perivenular lymphocytic cuff inside the plaque
many small nuclei in the plaque (macrophages, gliosis)
images.author: Marvin 101
images.credit: Marvin 101, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Gram stain of cloudy CSF in meningococcal meningitis: many neutrophils with small pink Gram-negative diplococci, some inside the cells. This finding justifies immediate antibiotics and prophylaxis for close contacts.
images.author: Microman12345
images.credit: Microman12345, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: India ink preparation of Cryptococcus neoformans. The ink particles cannot enter the thick polysaccharide capsule, so each round yeast sits in a clear halo; this is a classic test in HIV-associated meningitis.
look_for: wide clear halo (capsule) excluding the ink
images.author: CDC/Dr. Leanor Haley
images.credit: CDC/Dr. Leanor Haley, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Small bowel biopsy in coeliac disease with total villous atrophy: the surface is flat and the crypts are long and crowded (Marsh 3). Gluten-driven T-cell injury destroys the absorptive villi, causing malabsorption.
look_for: flat mucosal surface with no villi
lamina propria crowded with lymphocytes and plasma cells
images.author: Ed Uthman from Houston, TX, USA
images.credit: Ed Uthman from Houston, TX, USA, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Higher power of the coeliac biopsy: small dark lymphocytes sit between the surface enterocytes. More than about 25 intraepithelial lymphocytes per 100 enterocytes is the earliest Marsh lesion and persists in villous atrophy.
look_for: small round intraepithelial lymphocytes among enterocytes
images.author: Ed Uthman from Houston, TX, USA
images.credit: Ed Uthman from Houston, TX, USA, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Normal oesophageal lining of non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium, with a dark basal layer that matures upward into flattened surface cells. This tough layer resists abrasion from food but not acid reflux.
look_for: basal cell layer with dark crowded nuclei
images.author: Samir@enwiki
images.credit: Samir@enwiki, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Barrett oesophagus: squamous lining (left) gives way to columnar mucosa with goblet cells, intestinal metaplasia caused by chronic reflux. Goblet cells confirm the diagnosis and mark an increased risk of adenocarcinoma.
look_for: goblet cells with clear mucin vacuoles
glandular crypts in the lamina propria
images.author: Mikael Häggström, M.D.
images.credit: Mikael Häggström, M.D., CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Normal oxyntic gastric mucosa: short foveolar pits lined by mucous cells lead to long glands packed with pink parietal cells and bluish chief cells. Parietal cells secrete acid and intrinsic factor; chief cells secrete pepsinogen.
look_for: surface foveolar cells with mucin caps
pink parietal cells in the upper glands
basophilic chief cells deeper in the glands
images.author: Nephron
images.credit: Nephron, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: At very high power, Helicobacter pylori appear as tiny curved rods in the mucus layer above the foveolar cells. Their urease neutralises acid locally, and chronic infection causes gastritis, peptic ulcers and gastric cancer risk.
look_for: small curved rods in the surface mucus
organisms hugging the foveolar cell surface
inflammatory cells in the lamina propria
images.author: Nephron
images.credit: Nephron, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Normal duodenal biopsy with tall finger-like villi and short crypts, a villus-to-crypt ratio of about 3 to 4:1. Compare with the flat coeliac biopsy to see what villous atrophy removes.
look_for: villus-to-crypt height ratio around 3:1 or more
images.author: CoRus13
images.credit: CoRus13, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Close-up of normal villi lined by tall absorptive enterocytes with a brush border and scattered goblet cells. Only a few lymphocytes sit in the epithelium, unlike the crowded epithelium of coeliac disease.
look_for: tall columnar enterocytes with a pink brush border
images.author: CoRus13
images.credit: CoRus13, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Colonic biopsy in Crohn disease with a non-caseating granuloma at the base of the mucosa. A granuloma without caseation helps separate Crohn disease from ulcerative colitis.
look_for: tight cluster of epithelioid histiocytes with no central necrosis
chronic inflammation in the lamina propria
images.author: Nephron
images.credit: Nephron, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Duodenal biopsy with Giardia trophozoites in the lumen next to intact villi. The pear-shaped parasites cling to the brush border with a ventral disc and cause malabsorptive diarrhoea, often with near-normal histology.
look_for: pear or sickle-shaped trophozoites in the lumen
images.author: Nephron
images.credit: Nephron, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Active ulcerative colitis: a crypt lumen filled with neutrophils (crypt abscess) amid a dense plasma-cell-rich lamina propria. Disease confined to the mucosa, starting in the rectum and spreading continuously, is typical of UC.
look_for: crypt lumen packed with neutrophils (crypt abscess)
plasma cells crowding the lamina propria
images.author: CoRus13
images.credit: CoRus13, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Colorectal tubular adenoma: the dysplastic crypts on one side are crowded and dark with elongated nuclei, beside normal crypts full of goblet cells. Adenomas are the main precursor of colorectal cancer, which is why polyps are removed at colonoscopy.
look_for: crowded crypts with dark pencil-shaped nuclei
loss of goblet cell mucin in dysplastic crypts
abrupt transition to normal colonic crypts
images.author: Nephron
images.credit: Nephron, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Invasive colorectal adenocarcinoma: irregular malignant glands with central 'dirty' necrosis invade the wall next to residual normal mucosa. Depth of invasion and nodal spread set the stage and treatment.
look_for: normal crypts at the edge for comparison
images.author: Nephron
images.credit: Nephron, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Pseudomembranous colitis from Clostridioides difficile toxin: fibrin, mucus and neutrophils erupt from damaged crypts in a 'volcano' and spread as a pseudomembrane over the surface. It usually follows antibiotic use.
look_for: mushroom or volcano-shaped exudate over the mucosa
fibrin, mucus and neutrophil debris in the plume
images.author: Ed Uthman from Houston, TX, USA
images.credit: Ed Uthman from Houston, TX, USA, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Cultured Giardia trophozoites stained with Giemsa. Each pear-shaped organism has two nuclei that look like eyes, a central axostyle and trailing flagella, which give it a face-like appearance.
images.author: Eva Nohýnková
images.credit: Eva Nohýnková, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: A single Giardia trophozoite at high power showing its paired nuclei, curved median bodies and four pairs of flagella. The ventral sucking disc lets it attach to the duodenal brush border.
look_for: two nuclei at the broad front end
images.author: Stefan Walkowski
images.credit: Stefan Walkowski, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Scanning electron micrograph of Clostridioides difficile rods from a stool sample. This spore-forming anaerobe overgrows when antibiotics disrupt colonic flora, and its toxins A and B cause pseudomembranous colitis.
look_for: cells in clumps and short chains
images.author: CDC (Public Health Image Library)
images.credit: CDC (Public Health Image Library), public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Gram stain of Escherichia coli from culture: short pink Gram-negative rods. The thin peptidoglycan layer loses crystal violet during decolourisation and takes up the safranin counterstain.
images.author: Bobjgalindo
images.credit: Bobjgalindo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Gram stain of Salmonella Typhimurium: Gram-negative rods that look like E. coli on a smear. They are separated by culture and biochemistry (non-lactose fermenting, H2S producing), not by the Gram stain.
images.author: Y tambe
images.credit: Y tambe, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Giemsa stain of a gastric biopsy: Helicobacter pylori show as dark blue curved rods in the mucus over the foveolar epithelium. Special stains make scanty organisms far easier to find than on H&E.
look_for: small dark curved or S-shaped rods
organisms in surface mucus and pits
images.author: Ed Uthman from Houston, TX, USA
images.credit: Ed Uthman from Houston, TX, USA, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Normal lung: a small bronchiole with folded epithelium and a smooth-muscle cuff, surrounded by thin-walled alveoli. The delicate alveolar septa carry the capillaries for gas exchange.
look_for: bronchiole with ciliated epithelium and smooth muscle
thin alveolar septa enclosing empty air spaces
images.author: Yale Rosen from USA
images.credit: Yale Rosen from USA, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Normal bronchial wall with pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium on top and seromucous glands with a duct in the submucosa. Cilia and mucus together form the mucociliary escalator that clears inhaled particles.
look_for: pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells
thin basement membrane under the epithelium
images.author: Yale Rosen from USA
images.credit: Yale Rosen from USA, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Acute bacterial pneumonia at low power: alveoli in the lower half are filled solid with inflammatory exudate while the upper lung is still aerated. This consolidation is what produces dullness to percussion and an opacity on chest X-ray.
look_for: aerated lung next to consolidated lung
alveolar walls preserved around the exudate
images.author: Nephron
images.credit: Nephron, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Higher power of the same pneumonia: alveolar spaces are full of neutrophils with fibrin and some red cells, while the septa stay intact. Intact walls are why the lung can heal back to normal after the infection clears.
look_for: strands of fibrin and red cells in the exudate
images.author: Nephron
images.credit: Nephron, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Severe emphysema: alveolar walls are destroyed, leaving large air spaces with free-floating septal stubs. Loss of surface area and elastic recoil causes air trapping and impaired gas exchange in COPD.
images.author: Mikael Häggström, M.D.
images.credit: Mikael Häggström, M.D., CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Pulmonary tuberculosis with a necrotising granuloma next to an airway. Bacilli arrive by inhalation, so granulomas often centre on bronchioles; caseous centres can erode into airways and seed cavities.
look_for: granuloma with a central necrotic zone
epithelioid histiocytes and lymphocytes around the necrosis
images.author: Yale Rosen from USA
images.credit: Yale Rosen from USA, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung with a keratin pearl: concentric layers of pink keratin inside a nest of atypical squamous cells. It arises centrally in smokers' bronchi and can secrete PTHrP causing hypercalcaemia.
look_for: large polygonal cells with glassy pink cytoplasm
images.author: Nephron
images.credit: Nephron, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Bronchiole from a patient with asthma: the lumen is plugged by mucus, the epithelium has many goblet cells and the wall is thickened with inflammation. Mucus plugging and smooth-muscle constriction cause the airflow limitation.
look_for: mucus plug filling the airway lumen
thickened basement membrane and inflamed wall
images.author: Yale Rosen
images.credit: Yale Rosen, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Lung adenocarcinoma, acinar pattern: malignant glands of atypical cells infiltrate the lung. Adenocarcinoma is the commonest lung cancer, arises peripherally and also occurs in never-smokers; EGFR or ALK changes guide targeted therapy.
look_for: irregular glands lined by atypical columnar cells
images.author: Librepath
images.credit: Librepath, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Ziehl-Neelsen stain of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid: red acid-fast bacilli of Mycobacterium tuberculosis stand out against blue cells. A positive smear means the patient is likely infectious.
look_for: bacilli lying singly and in loose clumps
images.author: Ajay Kumar Chaurasiya
images.credit: Ajay Kumar Chaurasiya, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Gram stain of Streptococcus pneumoniae: purple Gram-positive cocci in pairs, each pair slightly pointed at the ends (lancet-shaped). Pneumococcus is the commonest cause of community-acquired lobar pneumonia.
images.author: Arnold Kaufman
images.credit: Arnold Kaufman, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Gram stain of Klebsiella from culture: plump pink Gram-negative rods. Klebsiella pneumoniae causes aspiration and hospital pneumonia, classically in alcohol use disorder, and many strains carry carbapenemases.
images.author: Ajay Kumar Chaurasiya
images.credit: Ajay Kumar Chaurasiya, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Silver stain showing Pneumocystis jirovecii cysts as dark round to cup-shaped bodies. Pneumocystis pneumonia is a defining opportunistic infection when CD4 counts fall below 200 cells/µL. (The organism was formerly called P. carinii.)
look_for: round or crescent cup-shaped black cysts
cysts about the size of a red cell
clusters of cysts in a foamy background
images.author: CDC (Public Health Image Library)
images.credit: CDC (Public Health Image Library), public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: GMS stain of angioinvasive aspergillosis with black hyphae invading a vessel. Aspergillus hyphae are narrow, septate and branch at acute angles, and vessel invasion leads to infarction in neutropenic patients.
look_for: hyphae within and through the vessel wall
images.author: Yale Rosen from USA
images.credit: Yale Rosen from USA, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Scanning electron micrograph of a pneumococcal diplococcus. Its polysaccharide capsule resists phagocytosis and is the target of pneumococcal vaccines.
look_for: pores in the filter membrane behind
images.author: Janice Haney Carr
images.credit: Janice Haney Carr, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Normal glomerulus on PAS, which outlines basement membranes in magenta. Thin, delicate capillary loops sit inside Bowman's space and capsule, surrounded by proximal tubules with brush borders.
look_for: thin, even capillary loop basement membranes
proximal tubules with PAS-positive brush borders
images.author: Ed Uthman, MD
images.credit: Ed Uthman, MD, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Crescentic glomerulonephritis: proliferating parietal epithelial cells and macrophages form a crescent in Bowman's space that compresses the glomerular tuft. Crescents mean severe capillary wall rupture and rapidly progressive renal failure.
images.author: Nephron
images.credit: Nephron, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Post-infectious glomerulonephritis: the glomerulus is enlarged and hypercellular with neutrophils in the capillary loops. Immune complexes formed after a streptococcal infection deposit in the glomerulus, causing haematuria, oedema and hypertension.
images.author: Nephron
images.credit: Nephron, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma: nests of cells with clear cytoplasm (lipid and glycogen dissolve in processing) separated by a rich network of thin blood vessels. Loss of VHL activates hypoxia signalling, which drives that vascularity.
look_for: cells with clear or pale cytoplasm and distinct borders
images.author: Nephron
images.credit: Nephron, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Acute pyelonephritis: neutrophils flood the interstitium and tubules around a spared glomerulus. Ascending infection, usually E. coli, causes fever, flank pain and white cell casts in urine.
look_for: dense neutrophilic infiltrate in the interstitium
images.author: Nephron
images.credit: Nephron, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Diabetic glomerulosclerosis with a Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodule: a round PAS-positive mesangial nodule pushing capillary loops aside. Long-standing hyperglycaemia thickens basement membranes and expands the mesangium, leading to proteinuria and chronic kidney disease.
look_for: thickened capillary and Bowman's capsule basement membranes
compressed capillary loops at the edge of the nodule
images.author: KGH
images.credit: KGH, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Acute tubular injury: proximal tubules have flattened epithelium, lost brush borders and sloughed cells or debris in their lumens, while the glomerulus looks normal. Ischaemia or toxins cause this, and it is a leading cause of hospital acute kidney injury and can follow severe volume depletion such as in DKA.
images.author: Amadalvarez
images.credit: Amadalvarez, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Gram stain of Escherichia coli, the commonest cause of urinary tract infection and pyelonephritis. Fimbriae (P pili) let uropathogenic strains climb the urinary tract and attach to urothelium.
images.author: Dr Graham Beards
images.credit: Dr Graham Beards, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Unstained urine sediment with a white blood cell cast: leucocytes trapped in a protein cylinder moulded in a renal tubule. Because casts form in tubules, WBC casts place the inflammation in the kidney, as in pyelonephritis or interstitial nephritis.
look_for: round granular leucocytes inside the cast
lobed nuclei visible in some cells
images.author: Ajay Kumar Chaurasiya
images.credit: Ajay Kumar Chaurasiya, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
